title: NBA’s Terry Rozier investigation could become part of illegal gambling trial
content:
The NBA’s investigation into veteran guard Terry Rozier for alleged sports gambling may become part of the government’s case at trial next year.

Lawyers for the Department of Justice have asked the federal judge overseeing the case to allow evidence that Rozier lied during the course of the NBA’s investigation into whether Rozier took himself out early from a March 2023 Charlotte Hornets game as part of an illegal gambling scheme. Attorneys for Rozier asked the judge to compel the NBA to hand over the full results of that investigation if prosecutors intend to use parts of it at trial and say that the league has so far only shared outlines of it orally and not its entire report.

The NBA’s role in the Rozier case, and what it found during its investigation three years ago, became a focal point of the federal case this week after attorneys for Rozier and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of New York traded legal filings that each asked Judge LaShann DeArcy Hall to access the NBA’s investigation as part of their case.

Federal prosecutors said that Rozier lied during the NBA’s investigation and want Hall to allow that alleged evidence during trial, which is scheduled to begin Feb. 8. Rozier and Deniro Laster, his longtime friend who was also charged last fall, are the only remaining defendants who have not pleaded guilty to charges in what the government alleged was a scheme centered on Rozier agreeing to take a $100,000 payoff to take himself out early from that Hornets game so that bettors could win their wagers on his statistics. Both have pleaded not guilty and were out on bond. Laster was taken into custody in August after Hall found that he had tried to tamper with witnesses.

“It is our understanding that no NBA player other than Terry Rozier is alleged to have engaged in any misconduct related to the gambling scheme claimed to have been perpetrated by Rozier and Deniro Laster,” an NBA spokesperson said. “We continue to cooperate with the government’s investigation.”

Rozier, the prosecutors allege, told the NBA during its investigation that he did not know Laster’s sister or that Laster had a sister, despite Rozier’s close relationship with Laster and that he had her number in his phone. Laster’s sister bet on Rozier for that game, according to the filing, and Rozier has paid for her legal fees.

Federal prosecutors have also asked the judge to allow evidence during the trial that Rozier deleted messages with alleged co-conspirators during the league’s investigation and did not give over his second phone to investigators.

The NBA’s investigation did not find that Rozier had committed any wrongdoing, and the league let him continue playing for two more seasons before he was arrested last October. The league’s investigation remains open. Government lawyers have asked Hall not to allow evidence at the trial that would reveal the NBA’s investigation didn’t find Rozier had broken its rules.

Lawyers for Rozier said that the NBA has only described portions of its findings and only orally. They have asked the judge to force the NBA to hand over the league’s full report on its investigation, as well as interview notes about the case, if federal prosecutors intend to rely on what the league found.

“The NBA is cooperating with the government. It has shared the substance of the interview. The government plans to build part of its case on the NBA’s investigation. The NBA’s file is within the government’s practical control. The government should be ordered to request it and produce it,” Rozier’s lawyers said in the latest court filing. They added, “If the government puts any part of the NBA investigation before the jury, the defense is entitled to the entire file.”

The two sides are also at odds about a text message Laster sent after the March 23, 2023, game. David Markus, Rozier’s lawyer, has said that the message from Laster to another man, which said, “Dont tell chum bout the bet,” proves Rozier’s innocence. Rozier is nicknamed Chum, and his lawyers say that the text shows that Laster had not involved the then-Hornets guard in the scheme.

Laster is accused of selling information about Rozier to a group of sports bettors. Several of them have already pleaded guilty, including Marves Fairley, who told a federal judge that he paid an NBA player to manipulate his performance. While Fairley did not name Rozier, David Berman, a lawyer for the Eastern District of New York, told the judge that Rozier was the player Fairley described.

Prosecutors say the man who received that text has told them that it was not about the betting scheme around that Hornets game in March.

Federal prosecutors allege that the plot around Rozier began the month prior and that he agreed then to take money in exchange for scoring fewer points. The bettors settled on the March 23 Hornets-Pelicans game days before it was played and just before tipoff, prosecutors said in the filing, they told Laster that Rozier would have to hit the under on other prop bets on his stats. Rozier left the game after he played nine minutes and 34 seconds and did not return because of a foot injury, and did not play again that season. He ended the game with fewer points, assists and 3-pointers than the betting lines on him, but went over on rebounds.

Afterward, according to Thursday’s filing, an alleged unnamed co-conspirator texted Laster, “No way bro … U didn’t tell him.”

Prosecutors say that in early April, Laster texted Fairley and told him that he and Rozier were trying to set up one of Rozier’s Hornets teammates to participate in another bet, also wagering on under. Laster, according to the filing, also contacted another NBA player he knew with an offer.

“(Let me know) if u tryna make 100k gang,” he wrote.

Rozier has not played in the NBA since the 2024-25 season. He was arrested the morning after the Miami Heat’s season opener last season and was put on leave. He is a free agent, though his lawyers have told the judge that he hopes to get back into the NBA.

He is one of five current or former NBA players who have been indicted since the summer of 2024 for their alleged roles in gambling cases involving NBA games. Damon Jones, an 11-year NBA vet, pleaded guilty to selling non-public information to a group of gamblers. Malik Beasley and Ed Davis intend to plead guilty in a related case in which Davis has been accused of orchestrating a gambling scheme that wagered on Beasley as he allegedly manipulated his performance during four games with the Milwaukee Bucks in the 2023-24 season. Jontay Porter pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud in 2025.
